transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-07 14:00 PDT
Duration: 55 mins
Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Jonas (Redwood SE), Aisha (Redwood SE), Priya (BrightEdge), Marcus (BrightEdge SRE), Ethan (Platform), Laura (CTO)
Links referenced: https://redwoodai.com/decks/kv-batch-smoke (deck), https://sheets.example.com/brightedge-latency (bench spreadsheet), runbook: internal/redwood/runbooks/kvcache-prefetch.md

[00:00] Samira: hey everyone thanks for joining uh we'll kick off, I know you wanted a really hands-on look at latency and kernel choices given your VPC/onprem constraints, so jonas and aisha will run through live-ish traces and a few stress patterns.
[00:18] Priya: yep thanks, we wanna understand why we saw those p95 spikes during our last smoke test, and whether ttrt-llm drivers or vLLM path will be better for our mixed-chat workload.
[00:30] Jonas: cool, quick agenda, we'll show a short trace where cuda graph replay fails on resume, then kv-cache priming behavior, batching lane sizing, and a couple of quant runs INT8. this is not exhaustive, just a focused triage.
[00:45] Marcus: one thing up front our env is kinda hybrid, it's a VPC with host devices exposed for the onprem rack via SR-IOV, latency sensitive but also token cost matters.
[01:02] Aisha: noted. right there is where we see networking jitter sometimes make cudagraph replays blow up if stream ordering changes, so we'll show how that looks.
[01:20] Laura: do you expect nvlink differences to matter here? our racks will be single-socket A40 w/ 48GB and an nvlink patch planned later.
[01:32] Jonas: yes nvlink changes the kernel routing and memory bank affinity. with single socket the kernel selection tends to pick smaller workspace kernels and fewer fused kernels in TRT-LLM, vLLM sometimes keeps larger fused kernels but uses different launch configs.
[01:50] Priya: sorry when you say fused kernels you mean fused attention and feedforward ops?
[02:00] Jonas: yeah fused attention + mlp. TRT tends to prefer a fused attention with lower launch count, vLLM's path uses dynamic attention kernels that optimize for short sequences but can thrash for long ones.
[02:18] Samira: show us the timeline trace please.
[02:25] Jonas: sharing trace, umm in the first 90s you'll see a cudaGraph capture then we pause and resume; at resume we got a cudaErrorLaunchTimeout on one of the fused kernels, it retries and then falls back to the generic kernel path which doubles p95.
[02:45] Ethan: is that because the graph's captured stream ordering doesn't match net rx arrivals in VPC?
[02:54] Jonas: in our repro yes, if the NIC batches traffic into different CUDA streams during the capture period the replay assumptions break. Also if KV cache is being primed in parallel it changes memory residency so the replayed graph's assumptions on persistent buffers fail.
[03:15] Marcus: ok that matches our observ: the spikes often follow rapid prime traffic from our multi-tenant aggregator.
[03:25] Aisha: so mitigation options: 1) prefer non-cudagraph mode for short-lived or highly variable stream arrivals; 2) use conservative cudagraph captures with explicit stream pinning and buffer residency hints; 3) pre-prime KV cache in a separate warmup window so replay sees stable residency.
[03:48] Priya: hmm pre-prime seems doable but we worry about cost. what's the CPU/GPU overhead for priming say 10k tokens?
[03:58] Jonas: rough numbers from our runbook: a 10k token prime at batch size 4 on an A40 is ~0.8 GPU-minutes and yields lower p95 in steady-state. We'll add exact numbers to the sheet.
[04:12] Samira: we'll attach the exact template and a cost calc.
[04:20] Jonas: moving to KV eviction: here's a 30s window where we intentionally change request distribution. you can see eviction thrash when cache size is slightly under working set, TRT-LLM's cache manager aggressively evicts older key blocks causing extra loads; vLLM uses LRU with prefetch heuristics that sometimes mitigate but can over-prefetch.
[04:45] Priya: over-prefetch sounds better than evicting constantly, but it ate memory in our test and then CUDA OOM happened.
[04:53] Jonas: exactly that's the tradeoff — prefetch reduces latency but increases memory pressure. our recommendation is adaptive prefetch with a memory headroom signal, which we can tune for your 48GB device.
[05:08] Marcus: can that headroom signal read free memory plus pinned buffers from other processes? our infra is multi-tenant.
[05:15] Aisha: we integrate with the node manager so yes, it reads device free memory and accounts for pinned KV regions, but in multi-tenant you get noisy neighbor pressure which is when we recommend reserved capacity or cgroups in die.
[05:30] Laura: so would Redwood Dedicated solve this, or are we better on a fine-tuned onprem deploy?
[05:40] Samira: Dedicated helps because we can guarantee device allocation and avoid noisy neighbors, but onprem with our Private package and strict device isolation can achieve similar determinism — tradeoffs are ops complexity vs control.
[05:55] Priya: let's talk quantization — we tried INT8 and saw a 1.8x throughput improvement but quality dropped on few-shot prompts. any kernel implications?
[06:05] Jonas: INT8 changes which kernels are available; some fused kernels in TRT-LLM have INT8 paths but they use calibration tables and can change launch parameters; in vLLM the INT8 path sometimes falls back to per-layer dequantize/requantize which increases launch overhead. so throughput improvements vary by model shape.
[06:26] Samira: can you run a quick microbench for our 7B chat model shape?
[06:32] Jonas: yes we can add that to the pilot. we'll run TRT-LLM INT8, vLLM INT8, and a fp16 baseline and collect per-kernel timings.
[06:40] Priya: when you run those will you include token-length skew? our distribution has many short tokens, a long tail at 512 tokens.
[06:48] Jonas: absolutely, we'll run mixed-length load with lane-based batching to emulate your p50/p95.
[06:55] Samira: quick interjection — on batching, our recommended lane sizing is dynamic lanes with a small hot lane for short requests and adaptive aggregation for long ones; static big batches reduce latency for throughput but hurt p95.
[07:12] Priya: can you explain how lane fission works again?
[07:20] Aisha: sure lane fission splits concurrency into lanes by expected seq length; short-lane packs many short requests and gets a fused short-seq kernel; long-lane schedules individually so it avoids padding blowup. this reduces token waste and can improve throughput while keeping p95 lower.
[07:40] Marcus: does cudagraph interact poorly with lane fission? we saw a crash earlier combining the two.
[07:48] Jonas: it can. cudagraph assumes a stable execution sequence; if lanes are dynamically fissioned during capture the graph's schedule won't reflect runtime ordering. solution: either capture per-lane graphs and switch at runtime with guarded checks, or avoid graphs for lanes that reconfigure frequently.
[08:05] Priya: that per-lane graph approach sounds complex. what's the ops burden?
[08:12] Jonas: moderate — we ship examples for graph per lane and a guard runtime that selects graph or dynamic path; we'll include the sample code in the runbook we share.
[08:24] Laura: about telemetry — what traces should we collect for the pilot?
[08:30] Aisha: per-request: kernel timings, cache hits/misses, cudaGraph replay events, memory residency markers, and NIC arrival timing. we'll give a small agent to capture and push to your prometheus endpoint.
[08:44] Marcus: do you keep any of that data? we need to ensure PII/data residency rules are respected.
[08:50] Samira: by default telemetry is ephemeral and we can disable any content-level traces; we'll use only performance meta. plus for Private deployments metrics can be forwarded to your internal stack.
[09:05] Priya: ok good. back to the earlier point on CUDA errors — can you reproduce the cudagraph error on our single-socket A40?
[09:12] Jonas: we reproduced locally on A40 when we toggled stream ordering and primed KV concurrently, the graph assumed certain persistent buffer pointers that changed at resume. we have a small repro we'll run in your env.
[09:28] Samira: action: jonas will create that repro image and provide exact driver/kernel pairs.
[09:34] Marcus: also we noticed a subtle difference in p95 when using our VPC vs local lab — maybe NIC offload timing is introducing microbursts.
[09:42] Jonas: NIC offload (TCP segmentation offload) can change packet arrival granularity; that will effect the runtime's request batching heuristics. for VPC we recommend disabling tso/gso on the probe interface during the pilot or instrumenting arrival times to adjust the batching window.
[09:58] Priya: can you quantify the batch window impact? a 5ms window vs 10ms?
[10:05] Aisha: in our tests, increasing window from 5ms to 10ms reduced GPU throughput variance but increased average latency by ~3-6ms depending on batch size. we'll show the sensitivity curves.
[10:20] Samira: ok let's move to the quant benchmark plan — what's the matrix?
[10:25] Jonas: matrix: TRT-LLM fp16, TRT-LLM INT8 (calib), vLLM fp16, vLLM INT8 (per-layer), and a conservative cudagraph vs non-cudagraph per path. we'll collect p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, kernel-level timings, memory headroom, and OOM events.
[10:45] Laura: are there any known failure modes when mixing INT8 and cudagraph?
[10:52] Jonas: yes when calibration tables reference different buffer layouts the graph can become invalid at resume; it's more likely if calibration alters quant scales per-batch. the safe approach is to avoid cudagraph for highly dynamic quantized flows or use calibration that is stable across expected token shapes.
[11:12] Priya: reasonable. how fast can you run this pilot and get results?
[11:18] Samira: we can stand up the script and agent in 3 business days after you share the benchmark sheet and confirm IP access; then 72 hours of runs to collect steady state plus stress windows. so about 10 business days to deliver initial artifacts.
[11:34] Marcus: firewall and peering are the blocker. we'll open a ticket for that after the call.
[11:40] Aisha: we'll also include a short how-to for adjusting lane sizing and prefetch knobs in your helm chart or deploy manifest.
[11:50] Jonas: last thing: fallbacks and graceful degradation — we recommend an automatic fallback policy: try TRT-LLM path, if cudaGraph replay fails or kernel launches error, fallback to vLLM dynamic path or smaller variant model. this keeps calls live albeit with higher latency.
[12:12] Priya: ok, implement fallback is critical for us. can Redwood ship a default policy?
[12:18] Samira: yes we have canned policies and we can customize thresholds. we'll include into the pilot config.
[12:27] Laura: next steps recap?
[12:30] Samira: recap: Redwood to share deck and sheet (Samira), SE team to provide repro image and kernel flags (Jonas), BrightEdge to share traffic profile + open firewall (Priya/Marcus), schedule pilot and follow-up next week.
[12:48] Priya: sounds good, thanks all.
[12:52] Marcus: thanks, we'll try to have firewall rules in 48 hours.
[12:56] Samira: great we'll ping calendar and drop the runbook.
[13:05] Aisha: thanks everyone.

End transcript.
